notes.meaning: David gives thanks with his whole heart. That means honest, eager praise, with nothing held back and no false front. He will sing out loud 'before the gods.' Christians have read this in different ways: before kings and rulers, before the angels, or in the face of false idols. In each reading, David is not ashamed to praise the true God in front of anyone.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic Bibles such as the Douay-Rheims read 'in the sight of the angels.' Augustine took the verse as singing God's praise before the angels.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the psalm was written after the exile, not by David. They point to an old Greek heading naming Haggai and Zechariah, and suggest a leader like Zerubbabel or Nehemiah.

notes.meaning: David bows toward God's house, the place where the ark (the holy chest of God's covenant) was kept. He worships God in the way God set up. Christians see Jesus as our 'temple,' the one we look to when we come to God. David praises God for his steady love and for keeping his promises. God's 'word' here is mainly his promise to David. God kept it in a way that shows his greatness more than anything else he had done.

differ.view: Some evangelicals take this line to mean that Scripture stands above every other way God shows himself. They see it as a reason to trust all of the Bible.
Others warn against reading this as God putting his word above his own character. They note that newer translations say God has lifted up both his name and his word above all things.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew of the last line is hard to read. Some scholars change a word in it, and the NET Bible reads 'exalted your promise above the entire sky.'

notes.meaning: David prayed, and God answered on that very day. God did not always take the trouble away. Instead he gave David inner strength and courage to bear it. That kind of answer is just as real, and it is a reason to give thanks.

David looks ahead. He sees kings everywhere praising God once they hear what God has said and done. This may first mean nearby kings, like Hiram, who saw God's care for David. Christians also read it as a picture of the nations coming to God through the good news about Jesus.

These kings will sing about the ways of the Lord. That means his wise plans and the way he cares for his people. God's glory is greater than the glory of any king. Those who walk in God's ways have good reason to sing as they go.

God is high above everything, yet he bends down to care for humble people. He listens to them and protects them. He also sees right through the proud, even from far away. He keeps them at a distance and is not fooled by their boasting.

Even God's people may walk right through the middle of trouble. But David trusts that God will give him fresh life and courage there. God reaches out his hand to hold back the anger of enemies. His strong right hand will bring rescue.

God finishes what he starts. Whatever good work he has begun in his people, he will carry through to the end (see Philippians 1:6). Our hope of keeping on rests on God's love that never ends, not on our own strength. That confidence does not stop David from praying. It moves him to pray all the more: 'Don't leave your work unfinished.'

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern translations read the first line differently. The NET has 'The LORD avenges me,' and the NIV has 'will vindicate me' (will clear my name and defend me).
